lessons.title: Networks, the Internet and Connectivity
lessons.description: LAN vs WAN, internet structure (IP and routers), wired vs wireless, and transmission time.
lessons.content_html:
Why Connect Computers?

A computer network is two or more devices linked so they can exchange data and share resources. Without networks, every device would be an island: no email, no video calls, no shared printing in a school, no cloud storage. Networks enable collaboration at every scale — from two laptops in a bedroom to millions of servers spanning continents.

The advantages of networking are substantial. Files can be shared instantly without physical media. A single internet connection can be shared across many devices. Centralised storage makes backups simpler and more reliable. Users can communicate in real time. The disadvantages include the cost of hardware and ongoing maintenance, the risk of spreading malware to every connected device simultaneously, and the need for security measures to protect shared data from unauthorised access.

LAN and WAN

A LAN (Local Area Network) covers a small geographical area — a school building, a hospital ward, an office floor. The hardware (cables, switches, routers) is typically owned and managed by the organisation itself. Because devices are physically close together and the infrastructure is dedicated, LANs generally offer high-speed, reliable connections.

A WAN (Wide Area Network) covers a wide geographic area, connecting multiple LANs across cities, countries, or continents. WANs rely on third-party telecommunications infrastructure — leased telephone lines, undersea fibre optic cables, and satellite links — so no single organisation owns the entire network. The internet is the largest example of a WAN.

Key Fact

LAN vs WAN in three contrasts: Scale — LAN covers a small area (e.g. one building); WAN covers a large area (e.g. an entire country). Ownership — LAN hardware is owned by one organisation; WAN infrastructure is shared across multiple parties. Speed — LANs typically offer faster, more consistent connections because devices are physically close; WAN speeds depend on leased telecommunications links and vary significantly.

Unity College has a LAN connecting its computers across the school campus. The switches and cabling are owned by the school, giving speeds of up to 1 gigabit per second. Students at home connect to the internet (a WAN) via their broadband provider — speeds vary from 10 to 900 Mbit/s depending on the type of connection and distance from the exchange. Notice that:

  • The school LAN is a single-owner, small-area network with dedicated infrastructure.
  • The internet is a WAN owned by many parties — the school pays its ISP for a leased connection into this larger network.
  • When a student at home uses the school’s virtual learning environment, their data travels first across their home LAN (router to device), then out across the WAN (internet), and into the school’s LAN at the other end.

How the Internet is Structured

The internet is a global network of interconnected networks. Two key elements hold it together: IP addressing and routers.

Every device on the internet is assigned an IP address (Internet Protocol address) — a unique identifier that acts like a postal address. When data is sent across the internet, each packet carries the source and destination IP address so that network equipment can forward it correctly.

router are the signposts of the internet. A router examines the destination IP address on each incoming packet and forwards it along the best available path towards its destination. Data sent from a device in Manchester to a server in New York may pass through many routers along the way, each making its own forwarding decision. This distributed design means the internet has no single point of failure — if one route is blocked, traffic can be rerouted.

Wired vs Wireless Connectivity

Wired networks use physical cables to carry data. Fibre optic cable transmits data as pulses of light and can achieve very high speeds (up to and beyond 1 Gbit/s) over long distances with minimal signal degradation. Copper cable (such as twisted-pair Ethernet cable) is cheaper and simpler to install but its speed and maximum range are more limited, and it is more vulnerable to electrical interference from nearby equipment.

Wireless networks transmit data using radio waves. The main benefit is mobility: devices can connect from anywhere within range without needing a physical cable. This makes wireless ideal for smartphones, tablets, and laptops that move around. However, wireless connections are generally slower and less reliable than their wired equivalents, more susceptible to interference from walls, other devices, and competing signals, potentially less secure because signals can be intercepted by anyone in range, and their quality degrades with distance from the access point.

Key Fact

Wired: faster, more reliable, more secure, less interference — but cables restrict mobility. Wireless: flexible and mobile — but slower, more interference, signals can be picked up by unauthorised devices, and range is limited. The characteristics that matter most are: speed, range, latency (the delay before data starts moving), and bandwidth (the amount of data that can be carried at once).

Network Speeds and Transmission Time

Network speeds are measured in bits per second. The units you need to know are:

  • kilobit per second (kbit/s) — 1,000 bits per second
  • megabit per second (Mbit/s) — 1,000,000 bits per second
  • gigabit per second (Gbit/s) — 1,000,000,000 bits per second

Note that network speeds use decimal (1000-based) prefixes here — not binary. These are the standard units for measuring data transfer rates.

You also need to be able to calculate how long it takes to transfer a file. The relationship is:

Transfer time (seconds) = File size (bits) ÷ Transfer rate (bits per second)

File sizes are often given in bytes; remember that 1 byte = 8 bits. Convert before you calculate.

Question: A student wants to upload a 25 MiB video file to a school server. The school’s wired network has an upload speed of 100 Mbit/s. How long will the transfer take?

Step 1 — Convert file size to bits:
File size = 25 MiB = 25 × 1024 × 1024 bytes = 26,214,400 bytes
In bits: 26,214,400 × 8 = 209,715,200 bits

Step 2 — Convert transfer rate to bits per second:
100 Mbit/s = 100,000,000 bits per second

Step 3 — Calculate time:
Time = 209,715,200 ÷ 100,000,000 = 2.097 seconds (approximately 2.1 seconds)

Check: Does the answer make sense? A 25 MiB file at 100 Mbit/s should take about 2 seconds — this is consistent with common experience of school network speeds. Notice that the file size is given in binary MiB (mebibytes) but network speed uses decimal Mbit/s; the units must be handled separately.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For Calculate questions on transmission time, the most common error is forgetting to multiply bytes by 8 to get bits before dividing by the transfer rate. Always show your working in three clear steps: (1) convert file size to bits, (2) write down the transfer rate in bits per second, (3) divide. A Describe question asking you to compare wired and wireless should name at least two characteristics (speed and interference, or range and reliability) — naming only one will lose marks. For a 4-mark Describe, give four separate points rather than expanding one point at length.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A LAN covers a small area under one organisation’s ownership; a WAN covers a large geographic area using shared telecommunications infrastructure. The internet is the largest WAN.
  • The internet is structured around IP addresses (unique device identifiers) and routers (devices that forward packets along the best path).
  • Wired networks offer faster, more reliable, more secure connections; wireless offers mobility at the cost of lower speed, greater interference, and reduced security. Transmission time = file size in bits ÷ transfer rate in bits per second.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a Wide Area Network (WAN)?
A) A network covering a small area such as a school building, owned by one organisation
B) A network that uses Bluetooth to connect personal devices over a short range
C) A network covering a large geographic area that relies on third-party telecommunications infrastructure
D) A network that connects two computers in the same room using a cable
practice_questions.marks: C) A network covering a large geographic area that relies on third-party telecommunications infrastructure [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one characteristic of a wired network that makes it more suitable than a wireless network for a school’s computer lab.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: higher speed / more reliable / more secure / less susceptible to interference [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term IP address.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A numerical label assigned to every device on a network, used to uniquely identify and locate it so that data packets can be correctly routed to their destination.
Secure: A unique identifier for a device on a network used for routing.
Developing: A number that identifies a device on the internet.
Emerging: A device address (too vague). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which a wireless network connection differs from a wired network connection.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Any two contrasts, each clearly explained: (1) Wireless transmits data using radio waves whereas wired uses physical cables — meaning wireless devices can move freely but wired devices are fixed. (2) Wireless connections are generally slower and more susceptible to interference from walls and competing signals, whereas wired connections are faster and more reliable. (3) Wireless signals can be picked up by any device in range, making unauthorised access easier than with a wired connection. (4) Wireless range is limited by distance from the access point.
Secure: Two contrasts identified with reasonable detail.
Developing: Two differences stated without development.
Emerging: One difference stated. [2 marks per difference]

practice_questions.text: A software developer needs to upload a 400 MiB project file to a remote server. The upload speed of their internet connection is 80 Mbit/s. Calculate how long the upload will take. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Step 1 — File size in bytes: 400 × 1024 × 1024 = 419,430,400 bytes. Step 2 — Convert to bits: 419,430,400 × 8 = 3,355,443,200 bits. Step 3 — Divide by rate: 3,355,443,200 ÷ 80,000,000 = 41.94 seconds (approximately 42 seconds). Award method marks for correct approach even if arithmetic error.
Secure: Correct method shown; minor arithmetic error at most.
Developing: Correctly converts bytes to bits OR correctly divides but not both.
Emerging: Sets up the division but uses incorrect units throughout. [3 marks: 1 mark per correct step]

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of routers in making the internet work.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A router reads the destination IP address on each incoming data packet and forwards it along the best available path towards that destination. Routers connect multiple networks together and make routing decisions independently at each hop. Because there is no single central router, if one route is unavailable the traffic can be redirected along an alternative path — making the internet resilient.
Secure: Correctly explains packet forwarding and path selection; mentions IP addresses.
Developing: States routers direct traffic but does not explain how (IP addressing or path selection).
Emerging: Describes a router as connecting the internet without explaining its function. [4 marks]

A network covering a relatively small geographical area such as a single building or campus, usually owned and managed by one organisation.
A network covering a large geographic area, connecting multiple LANs across cities, countries or continents using third-party telecommunications infrastructure.

A networking device that forwards data packets between networks, reading the destination IP address and choosing the best path to send the packet towards its destination.
The maximum amount of data that can be transmitted over a network connection in a given period, measured in bits per second.

lessons.title: Network Protocols and the TCP/IP Model
lessons.description: What protocols are, the full protocol list (HTTP to IMAP), and the TCP/IP four-layer model.
lessons.content_html:
Why Protocols Are Necessary

Every time a web page loads or an email arrives, devices made by different manufacturers, running different operating systems, exchange data seamlessly. This works because of network protocol — agreed sets of rules that all devices follow when communicating. Without protocols, a phone made by one company could not send a message to a laptop made by another. Protocols create a common language for devices that would otherwise have nothing in common.

Protocols define many aspects of communication: how data is broken into chunks (packets), how packets are addressed, how errors are detected, and how the two ends of a connection signal that they have finished. Different tasks require different protocols — browsing the web uses different rules from sending an email, which uses different rules from transferring a large file. This is why several protocols coexist and each has its own specific purpose.

Key Fact

The protocols you must know: Ethernet (wired LAN data transmission), Wi-Fi (wireless LAN data transmission), TCP/IP (reliable internet transmission), HTTP (web page transfer), HTTPS (encrypted web transfer), FTP (file transfer between computers), SMTP (sending email), POP3 (retrieving email — downloads and deletes from server), IMAP (retrieving email — keeps on server, syncs across devices).

Protocols in Detail

Ethernet is the standard protocol for wired LANs. It defines the rules for transmitting data across a physical cable and uses MAC addresses (hardware addresses built into each network interface card) to identify devices on the same local network segment. When your computer sends data to another device on the same LAN, Ethernet handles the local delivery.

Wi-Fi is the wireless equivalent of Ethernet. It governs how devices communicate over radio waves within a local area. Like Ethernet, Wi-Fi uses MAC addresses to direct data on the local network. The key differences are the transmission medium (radio waves instead of cable) and the added challenge of managing shared radio spectrum fairly among multiple devices.

TCP/IP is really two protocols working together. IP (Internet Protocol) assigns addresses to devices and routes packets across networks. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) sets up the connection, splits data into numbered packets, checks they all arrive in order, and requests retransmission of any packet that is lost or corrupted. Together they form the backbone of internet communication.

HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) defines how a web browser requests a web page and how the server sends it back. When you type a web address, your browser sends an HTTP request; the server responds with the HTML content of the page. HTTP transmits data without encryption — the content can be read by anyone who intercepts the connection.

HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) adds encryption to HTTP. The data exchanged between browser and server is scrambled, so intercepting it reveals nothing useful. HTTPS is essential for any page that handles sensitive data — online banking, shopping checkouts, login forms. Look for the padlock icon in a browser’s address bar to confirm HTTPS is in use.

FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is designed specifically for moving files between a client and a server. Web developers use FTP to upload website files to a web hosting server; IT teams use it to distribute software updates across a network. FTP separates the control connection (commands) from the data connection (the file itself), running them on different network ports.

SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) handles the sending of email. When you press Send, your email application uses SMTP to submit your message to your outgoing mail server. SMTP is also used between mail servers to relay messages from the sender’s server to the recipient’s server.

POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3) retrieves emails from a mail server by downloading them to the local device. By default, messages are deleted from the server once downloaded — so if you read email on your phone using POP3, it will not appear on your laptop. POP3 suits users who only access email from one device.

IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) leaves emails on the server and synchronises the state across all devices. If you read an email on your phone, it is marked as read on your laptop too. If you delete it, it disappears everywhere. IMAP is the standard approach for anyone using email on multiple devices — phones, tablets, laptops and desktops all see the same inbox.

The key distinction to remember: SMTP sends; POP3 downloads and typically removes from server; IMAP keeps on server and syncs everywhere.

The Four-Layer TCP/IP Model

When data travels across the internet, the process is organised into four distinct layers. Each layer handles a specific job. Together, they form the TCP/IP model. Using layers keeps the design modular: a new application protocol can be added without rewriting how packets are routed; the physical hardware can change without changing how applications work.

Key Fact

The four layers of the TCP/IP model (top to bottom): Application — where applications operate using protocols such as HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP3, IMAP. Transport — manages communication sessions and reliable delivery; TCP operates here. Internet — handles addressing and routing of packets; IP operates here. Link — the physical hardware layer; the network interface card (NIC), Ethernet and Wi-Fi operate here, using MAC addresses.

Application layer — this is where network applications such as web browsers, email clients and file transfer tools operate. The protocols at this layer — HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP3 and IMAP — define how those applications format and exchange data. When you open a web browser, you are interacting with the Application layer.

Transport layer — manages the communication session between two hosts. TCP operates here: it breaks data into packets, numbers them, and verifies that all packets arrive in the correct order. If a packet is lost, TCP requests that it be sent again. This is what makes TCP a “reliable” protocol. The Transport layer also handles flow control (adjusting the rate of transmission to avoid overwhelming the receiver).

Internet layer — handles addressing and routing. IP operates here: it attaches source and destination IP addresses to each packet and determines the best path through the network of routers to reach the destination. Every router on the internet operates at this layer, reading the IP address and forwarding the packet accordingly.

Link layer — the lowest layer, responsible for the physical transmission of data across a single network link. The network interface card (NIC) sits here. Ethernet (for wired connections) and Wi-Fi (for wireless) operate at this layer, using MAC addresses to deliver data on the local network. A common exam error is confusing MAC addresses at the Link layer with IP addresses at the Internet layer — they operate at different layers and serve different purposes.

Data flow: when sending data, the application at the top passes its data down through all four layers (Application → Transport → Internet → Link), each layer adding its own addressing information. The data then travels physically across the network and is passed back up through all four layers on the receiving device (Link → Internet → Transport → Application), which strips away each layer’s information to deliver the original message to the application.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Layer-to-protocol mapping is examined almost every year and is worth 4–6 marks. The most common error is placing IP at the Transport layer and TCP at the Internet layer — it’s the other way around: TCP is at Transport, IP is at Internet. For a Describe question about a specific protocol, always state what it does and which layer it operates at. For FTP and POP3 questions, be precise: FTP transfers files (not emails); POP3 downloads emails and by default removes them from the server (unlike IMAP which keeps them there).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Protocols are agreed rules that allow devices from different manufacturers to communicate. The key protocols are: Ethernet, Wi-Fi, TCP/IP, HTTP, HTTPS, FTP (file transfer), SMTP (send email), POP3 (retrieve and delete), IMAP (retrieve and sync).
  • The TCP/IP model has four layers: Application (HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP3, IMAP), Transport (TCP), Internet (IP), Link (NIC, Ethernet, Wi-Fi, MAC addresses).
  • MAC addresses operate at the Link layer for local delivery; IP addresses operate at the Internet layer for routing across networks. These are different concepts at different layers.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following protocols operates at the Internet layer of the TCP/IP model?
A) HTTP
B) TCP
C) SMTP
D) IP
practice_questions.marks: D) IP [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the protocol used to transfer files between a client and a server across a network.
practice_questions.marks: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term network protocol.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: An agreed set of rules that govern how data is formatted, addressed, transmitted and received across a network, allowing devices from different manufacturers and operating systems to communicate reliably.
Secure: A set of rules for communication between devices on a network.
Developing: Rules that devices follow when communicating.
Emerging: Something computers use to talk to each other (too vague). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between POP3 and IMAP for receiving email.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: POP3 downloads emails from the server to the local device and typically deletes them from the server — they are not accessible on other devices. IMAP keeps emails on the server and synchronises the state across all devices — reading, deleting or organising an email on one device is reflected on all others.
Secure: Key difference (server deletion vs server storage/sync) correctly identified.
Developing: One protocol correctly described; the other vague.
Emerging: Names both without meaningful comparison. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of the Link layer in the TCP/IP model and identify one protocol that operates at this layer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The Link layer is responsible for the physical transmission of data across a single network link (e.g. a cable or wireless channel). It uses MAC addresses — unique hardware addresses assigned to each NIC — to identify devices on the local network and deliver data to the correct one. One protocol at this layer: Ethernet (for wired connections) or Wi-Fi (for wireless). Correct explanation of MAC addresses at this layer, contrasted with IP addresses at the Internet layer.
Secure: Role correctly described with one protocol identified and brief MAC address explanation.
Developing: Layer role stated without explanation of MAC addresses; protocol identified.
Emerging: Vague description of the layer; protocol missing or incorrect. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using HTTPS instead of HTTP for a school’s online homework portal.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Advantages — HTTPS encrypts data in transit so student login credentials and submitted work cannot be read if intercepted; browser shows a padlock, building trust; protects against man-in-the-middle attacks. Disadvantages — slightly higher processing overhead (encryption and decryption take time and computing resource); requires a valid SSL/TLS certificate which has a cost and must be renewed; may be slightly slower for low-powered devices. Evaluates: for a portal handling sensitive student data, the security benefit of HTTPS outweighs the performance cost, making it the appropriate choice.
Secure: Both sides argued with at least two valid points each; conclusion reached.
Developing: Advantages well argued; disadvantages vague or only one identified.
Emerging: Only advantages or only disadvantages stated; no evaluation. [6 marks]

lessons.title: Network Topologies
lessons.description: Bus, star and mesh topologies: structure, advantages, disadvantages, and how to choose between them.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Network Topology?

A network topology describes how the devices in a network are connected and how data travels between them. Choosing the right topology involves trade-offs: a design that minimises cabling cost may create a single point of failure; a design that is highly resilient may be expensive to install and maintain. The three topologies you must know are bus, star and mesh.

Understanding topologies matters for designing reliable networks. A small business setting up a new office will consider cost and ease of adding new machines. A hospital designing its patient-records network will prioritise reliability and fault tolerance. The “best” topology depends entirely on what the network is for.

Bus Topology

In a bus topology, all devices share one central cable — called the backbone or bus. When any device sends data, the signal travels along the backbone in both directions. Every device on the network receives the signal, but only the device with the matching address actually processes it. Terminators at each end of the backbone absorb signals so they do not bounce back.

Advantages:

  • Cheap to install — uses the least amount of cable of the three topologies, because all devices share one backbone.
  • Easy to add new devices — a new computer is simply connected to the backbone.
  • Simple to set up — no central switch or hub is required.

Disadvantages:

  • A single point of failure — if the backbone cable breaks, the entire network fails because there is no alternative path for data.
  • Performance degrades as more devices are added — all devices share the same bandwidth, so collisions become more frequent on a busy network.
  • Difficult to fault-find — a fault anywhere on the backbone is hard to isolate.
  • Not suitable for large networks because of bandwidth sharing and reliability issues.
Key Fact

In a bus topology, the backbone cable is a single point of failure. If it breaks, the entire network stops because there is no alternative path for data. This makes bus topology unsuitable for environments where continuous network access is critical.

Star Topology

In a star topology, each device has its own dedicated cable connecting it to a central switch (or hub). Data from any device travels to the switch, which reads the destination address and forwards the data only to the correct device. Modern networks almost universally use star topology for wired LANs.

Advantages:

  • Failure of one cable only affects the device on that cable — the rest of the network continues to function normally.
  • Fast performance — each device has a dedicated connection to the switch, so bandwidth is not shared in the same way as a bus.
  • Easy to add new devices — simply run a new cable from the device to the switch, without disrupting any existing connections.
  • Easy to identify faults — if a specific device loses connection, the problem is isolated to that device’s cable or connection.

Disadvantages:

  • The central switch is a single point of failure — if it breaks down, the entire network is disrupted because all communication passes through it.
  • More cable required than bus topology — each device needs its own run of cable to the central switch, which increases installation cost.
  • Cost of the central switch — a high-quality managed switch is an additional expense.

Mesh Topology

In a mesh topology, devices are interconnected with multiple paths between them. In a full mesh, every device connects to every other device directly. In a partial mesh, most devices have multiple connections but not every possible connection exists. The internet’s core infrastructure uses a partial mesh, which is why traffic can be re-routed around a failed link automatically.

Advantages:

  • Highly resilient — if one link or device fails, data can be re-routed via alternative paths. There is no single point of failure (in a full mesh).
  • Fast data transfer — data can take the shortest or least congested path between any two devices.
  • Highly scalable for high-reliability environments such as core internet infrastructure, hospital networks or military communications.

Disadvantages:

  • Very expensive to install — a full mesh of 10 devices requires 45 separate connections (the formula is n(n−1)÷2 connections for n devices).
  • Complicated to manage and configure — every device must be set up to handle multiple connections and routing decisions.
  • Uses a large amount of cable (for wired mesh) or radio spectrum (for wireless mesh), which adds to cost and complexity.
Key Fact

Topology comparison at a glance: Bus — cheapest, backbone is a single point of failure, poor scalability. Star — moderate cost, switch is a single point of failure but individual cable faults are isolated, most common for modern LANs. Mesh — most expensive, no single point of failure (full mesh), used for critical infrastructure requiring high resilience.

Scenario: A small café wants to connect five computers and a printer with the lowest possible installation cost. A hospital wants to connect its patient-records servers so that no single cable break can interrupt access.

Café: Bus topology is the cheapest option — one backbone cable serves all five computers and the printer. The café accepts the risk that a backbone fault will take down everything, because the cost saving is the priority and the network is small and not mission-critical.

Hospital: Mesh (or star with redundant links) is appropriate. Patient records are mission-critical: any network downtime could affect patient safety. The higher cost of multiple links is justified by the need for resilience. A full mesh of five servers requires only 10 connections: 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10 — manageable for a small cluster of critical servers.

Typical school LAN: Star topology. Each classroom computer has its own cable run to a central switch. If one cable is damaged, only that one computer is affected. Adding new computers is straightforward — run a new cable to the switch. The central switch is the only point of failure but can be replaced without rewiring the whole building.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Topology questions often ask you to describe a topology (2 marks) or explain why a particular topology is suitable for a given scenario (4 marks). For describe questions, give the structure (how devices are connected) as well as at least one characteristic (advantage or disadvantage). For explain questions, link the topology’s feature to the requirement in the scenario — for example, “a star topology is appropriate because if one cable fails, only that device is affected, meaning the network remains operational for all other users.” Name the specific topology — “a network with a central switch” will not score without identifying it as a star topology.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Bus topology: all devices share a single backbone cable. Cheapest but the backbone is a single point of failure and performance falls as devices are added.
  • Star topology: each device connects individually to a central switch. The most common modern LAN layout. A single cable failure only affects one device, but if the switch fails the whole network is disrupted.
  • Mesh topology: devices connect to multiple others via redundant paths. Highly resilient with no single point of failure (full mesh), but the most expensive and complex to install and manage.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following describes a bus topology?
A) Every device connects to a central switch with its own dedicated cable
B) All devices share a single central cable called the backbone
C) Every device connects directly to every other device
D) Devices are arranged in a ring with data travelling in one direction
practice_questions.marks: B) All devices share a single central cable called the backbone [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the single point of failure in a star topology.
practice_questions.marks: The central switch (or hub). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of a mesh topology.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In a mesh topology, each device connects to multiple other devices, creating redundant paths for data. A full mesh connects every device to every other device; a partial mesh provides multiple paths but not every possible connection. If one link fails, data can travel via an alternative route.
Secure: Multiple connections between devices and the concept of redundant paths identified.
Developing: States devices connect to multiple others but does not mention redundancy or full/partial mesh.
Emerging: Describes a topology with many connections but without accurate structural detail. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a star topology is more suitable than a bus topology for a school computer lab.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In a star topology, each computer has its own dedicated cable to the central switch. If one cable is damaged, only that computer loses its connection — the rest of the lab continues to work. In a bus topology, a single break in the backbone cable brings down the entire network. For a school environment where continuous access is important for lessons, the star topology’s fault isolation is a significant advantage. Adding new computers is also straightforward in a star (run a new cable to the switch) without disrupting existing connections.
Secure: Star topology’s fault isolation correctly explained and contrasted with bus backbone failure.
Developing: States star is better and gives a reason but does not explain the mechanism of fault isolation.
Emerging: Names star topology as more suitable without explanation. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two disadvantages of using a mesh topology for a small business network.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Any two of the following, each with detail: (1) Very high cabling and installation cost — a full mesh of n devices requires n(n-1)/2 connections, so adding each new device requires connecting it to every existing device. (2) Complex to configure and manage — each device must handle multiple connections and routing, requiring significant network administration expertise. (3) Uses a large amount of cable or wireless infrastructure, increasing both initial and ongoing costs.
Secure: Two distinct disadvantages identified with some development.
Developing: Two disadvantages stated without sufficient detail.
Emerging: One disadvantage stated. [2 marks each]

practice_questions.text: A company is setting up two networks: one connecting 20 office workstations for everyday tasks, and one connecting three mission-critical database servers that must remain accessible even if a link fails. Discuss which topology is most appropriate for each network.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Office workstations (star): each workstation has its own cable to a central switch. A single cable fault only affects one machine, keeping productivity loss minimal. The switch is the only single point of failure but is easy and inexpensive to replace. Cost is manageable (20 cable runs). Alternative view: mesh would give more resilience but is impractical for 20 office computers due to cost (190 connections needed). Database servers (mesh or partial mesh): three servers with full mesh requires only 3 connections but provides complete redundancy — any server or link can fail without losing access to the other servers. Small number of connections makes full mesh feasible here. Alternative view: star could work with a managed switch if the switch has a redundant power supply, but remains a single point of failure. Conclusion: star is most appropriate for the office (cost-effective, sufficient fault isolation); mesh is most appropriate for the servers (critical resilience requirement, small number of devices).
Secure: Both networks analysed with correct topology recommendation and reasoning; both sides of the argument considered for at least one network.
Developing: Both topologies correctly recommended with some reasoning; limited analysis of trade-offs.
Emerging: One network correctly analysed; the other vague or missing. [6 marks]

glossary_terms.definition: The physical or logical arrangement of devices in a network, defining how they are connected to each other and how data flows between them.
A network topology in which all devices are connected to a single central cable called the backbone. Data travels along the backbone until it reaches its destination device.
A network topology in which all devices connect individually to a central switch or hub. Data from any device travels to the switch, which forwards it to the correct destination.
A network topology in which each device connects to multiple other devices, creating redundant paths for data. A full mesh connects every device to every other device.
A single cable that all devices in a bus topology connect to and share for transmitting data.
A component whose failure brings down the entire network or system, leaving no alternative path for data.

lessons.title: Network Security
lessons.description: Finding network weaknesses via penetration testing and protecting with access control and firewalls.
lessons.content_html:
Why Network Security Matters

Every connected device is a potential target. A school network holds thousands of student and staff records. A hospital network carries patient data. A retail network processes payment details. network security is the combination of measures that protect these systems. A single unguarded entry point can expose an entire organisation’s data — which is why securing networks requires both identifying vulnerabilities before attackers do, and putting protections in place to prevent or limit damage if an attack occurs.

Network security thinking divides into two clear stages: identification (finding weaknesses) and protection (preventing or containing attacks). Both are equally important. A network that is well protected but never tested for new vulnerabilities will eventually be exploited through an overlooked weakness.

Identifying Vulnerabilities: Penetration Testing

penetration testing (often called “pen testing”) is the practice of deliberately attempting to break into a network or system — with the organisation’s knowledge and permission — to find security weaknesses. The goal is to discover vulnerabilities before a genuine attacker does, so they can be fixed. Penetration testers produce a detailed report of every weakness found, how it was exploited, and how to remediate it.

Penetration tests can target network infrastructure (routers, switches, firewalls), individual devices on the network, or the software running on those devices. A thorough pen test may include trying to intercept unencrypted network traffic, testing whether wireless access points accept weak passwords, or attempting to connect unauthorised devices to the network.

Key Fact

Penetration testing is only legal and ethical if the organisation explicitly authorises it in writing. The same techniques used in a pen test — scanning for open ports, attempting to bypass authentication, intercepting traffic — would be crimes under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 if carried out without permission. The authorisation is what transforms the activity from criminal hacking to a legitimate security service.

Identifying Vulnerabilities: Ethical Hacking

ethical hacking is the broader discipline of which penetration testing is one technique. An ethical hacker (sometimes called a white-hat hacker) has the same knowledge and tools as a malicious attacker but operates within a legal and ethical framework agreed with the client. Ethical hacking may also include social engineering tests (e.g. attempting to trick staff into revealing passwords), physical security tests (e.g. trying to enter a server room without authorisation), and code review to find software vulnerabilities.

The value of ethical hacking is in perspective: an external expert approaching a system with fresh eyes, using attacker techniques, will find vulnerabilities that internal IT staff who designed the system might overlook. Many organisations engage ethical hackers before launching a new network, after a significant change, or on a regular schedule.

A school contracts a security firm to conduct a penetration test of its network before the start of term. The testers are given written authorisation from the headteacher. Over three days, they:

  • Scan all network devices for open ports and identify three devices running outdated software with known security flaws.
  • Attempt to connect a laptop to the school Wi-Fi using default router credentials — and succeed, because the admin password had never been changed.
  • Attempt to access the server room by following a member of staff through the door — this “tailgating” attempt succeeds because the door was propped open.

Their report details all three vulnerabilities with recommendations: update the outdated software, change the router’s admin credentials, and enforce a strict door-closing policy. The school fixes all three before term begins. Without the pen test, any of these vulnerabilities could have been exploited by a malicious attacker.

Protecting Networks: Access Control

access control is the first line of protection: ensuring that only authorised users and devices can connect to the network, and that each user can only access the resources appropriate to their role. In a school, a student account might have access to shared homework folders but not to the administration system. A teacher account has broader access. A network administrator has the highest level of access.

Access control is implemented through user accounts and passwords, combined with user permissions that define what each account can do. Strong access control requires regularly reviewing who has which permissions, disabling accounts when users leave the organisation, and ensuring that users do not share accounts or passwords.

Protecting Networks: Physical Security

physical security protects the hardware that a network runs on. No amount of software-based security matters if an attacker can walk into a server room and physically remove a hard drive. Physical security measures include:

  • Locked server rooms — restricting entry to authorised personnel only, often using key cards, PIN pads or biometric readers on doors.
  • Cable management — securing network cables so they cannot be easily unplugged or tampered with.
  • Locked equipment — physically securing network switches and routers so they cannot be removed or reset.
  • CCTV and visitor logs — monitoring who enters secure areas and maintaining a record that can be reviewed after a security incident.

Protecting Networks: Firewalls

A firewall acts as a gatekeeper between a trusted internal network and an untrusted external one — typically the internet. It examines each data packet and decides, based on rules set by the network administrator, whether to allow it through or block it. A school might configure its firewall to block traffic to certain categories of website, reject all incoming connections on ports not used by school systems, and alert the administrator when unusual patterns of traffic are detected.

Packet filtering is the most common firewall technique: the firewall inspects the header of each packet (looking at source IP address, destination IP address, port number and protocol) and either allows or blocks it based on the rules. A packet from an unknown external IP address trying to connect to an internal database server on a port that should not be publicly accessible will be blocked. A packet from a trusted address connecting on an expected port will be allowed through.

Key Fact

Three categories of network protection: Access control — user accounts, passwords and permissions ensure only authorised users can connect and limit what they can do. Physical security — locked server rooms, secured cabling and equipment prevent physical tampering. Firewalls — inspect and filter packets based on rules, blocking unauthorised traffic between the internal network and external networks such as the internet.

Identification and protection are complementary, not alternatives. Access control, physical security and firewalls reduce the chance of a successful attack. But no defence is perfect: new vulnerabilities appear constantly as software changes, new devices are added and human behaviour varies. Penetration testing and ethical hacking identify weaknesses that protections have missed or that have developed since protections were last reviewed. A mature security strategy uses both: robust protections, tested regularly by independent experts who try to break them.

Example: a firewall may block most unauthorised traffic, but a pen test might discover that a misconfigured rule allows traffic through on an unexpected port. Without the pen test, this misconfiguration might go unnoticed until a malicious attacker finds it first.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For network security questions, the specification organises answers around two categories: identifying vulnerabilities (penetration testing, ethical hacking) and protecting networks (access control, physical security, firewalls). Structuring your answer around these two categories helps ensure you cover the right material. For an Explain question, always pair a statement of what the method does with a reason why it improves security — stating “a firewall blocks packets” scores one mark; adding “which prevents unauthorised external traffic from reaching internal systems, reducing the risk of a successful attack” scores the second. Never confuse penetration testing with malicious hacking in an exam answer — always state that it is authorised.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Identifying vulnerabilities: penetration testing and ethical hacking are authorised techniques that use attacker methods to find weaknesses before malicious actors do. The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes the same techniques criminal without explicit permission.
  • Protecting networks: access control (user accounts and permissions) restricts who can connect and what they can do; physical security (locked server rooms, secured hardware) prevents physical tampering; firewalls filter packets based on rules to block unauthorised traffic.
  • Identification and protection work together — protections reduce risk, and regular penetration testing finds the gaps that protections have missed.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes penetration testing?
A) Installing anti-malware software on all network devices
B) Monitoring network traffic to detect unusual patterns
C) Attempting to access a network without authorisation to expose vulnerabilities to malicious attackers
D) Attempting to gain access to a network with the organisation’s permission to identify security weaknesses
practice_questions.marks: D) Attempting to gain access to a network with the organisation’s permission to identify security weaknesses [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one example of a physical security measure used to protect network infrastructure.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: locked server room / key card or PIN access to server areas / CCTV in server rooms / cables secured and managed to prevent tampering / equipment physically locked to racks. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term firewall.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A network security device that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and decides whether to allow or block specific packets based on a set of predefined security rules, acting as a gatekeeper between a trusted internal network and an untrusted external network.
Secure: Monitors/filters network traffic based on rules; prevents unauthorised access.
Developing: A device that blocks unwanted internet traffic.
Emerging: Something that protects the network (too vague). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how access control is used to protect a school network.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Access control requires users to log in with a unique username and password to connect to the network. User permissions restrict what each account can do: student accounts may only access shared folders and the internet, while teacher accounts can access mark books and assessment data, and administrator accounts can change network settings. This ensures that even if an attacker gains access to one low-privilege account, they cannot access sensitive system files or other users’ data.
Secure: User accounts and permissions described with a school-appropriate example of different access levels.
Developing: States that users need passwords to log in; does not explain permissions.
Emerging: Vague description of restricting access without mechanism. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between penetration testing and ethical hacking.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Penetration testing is a specific technique within the broader discipline of ethical hacking — it involves attempting to access a network or system without legitimate credentials to find vulnerabilities, with written authorisation from the organisation. Ethical hacking is the broader practice that includes penetration testing but also social engineering tests (e.g. attempting to trick staff into giving up passwords), physical security tests (e.g. trying to enter a server room without authorisation), and software code review. Both involve using attacker techniques with permission, distinguishing them from criminal hacking.
Secure: Penetration testing correctly defined as a specific technique; ethical hacking correctly identified as the broader discipline, with at least one additional technique named.
Developing: Both terms described but the relationship (pen test is a type of ethical hacking) not made clear.
Emerging: Both described vaguely; no meaningful distinction. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the effectiveness of firewalls and physical security as methods of protecting a network, identifying the limitations of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Firewalls — effective at filtering malicious packets from external networks, can block traffic on specific ports and IP ranges, and can alert administrators to suspicious activity. Limitation: firewalls do not protect against threats already inside the network (e.g. an attacker who gains legitimate credentials), and sophisticated attacks may use allowed ports to bypass rules. Physical security — essential because software protections are useless if hardware can be physically removed. Locked server rooms prevent direct tampering; cable management prevents physical interception. Limitation: physical security only protects on-site infrastructure and relies on human behaviour (e.g. not holding doors open for others); it cannot protect data in transit across external networks. Overall: both methods are necessary but neither is sufficient alone — a well-designed network uses multiple overlapping layers of protection.
Secure: Both methods discussed with a valid limitation each; some comparison or evaluative comment.
Developing: Both methods described with one limitation between them; limited evaluation.
Emerging: Only one method discussed meaningfully. [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What makes penetration testing legal and ethical, rather than criminal?
options: Having explicit written authorisation from the organisation
Only testing your own personal devices

Access control restricts which _____ and devices can connect to a network and what they are permitted to do.

Match each network security method to its description:
right: Authorised attempts to break into a network to find vulnerabilities

glossary_terms.definition: The combination of processes, practices and technologies designed to protect a network, its infrastructure and the data it carries from unauthorised access, misuse or attack.

An authorised test in which security professionals attempt to gain access to a network or system without using legitimate credentials, in order to identify vulnerabilities before malicious attackers can exploit them.
The practice of using attacker techniques to find and expose vulnerabilities in a network or system, with explicit authorisation and the goal of improving security rather than causing harm.
A security mechanism that restricts which users and devices can connect to a network and what they are permitted to do, enforced through user accounts, passwords and permission levels.
The set of actions a user account is allowed to perform on a network or system, such as read, write, delete or execute, assigned by an administrator based on the user's role.
Measures that protect the physical infrastructure of a network from unauthorised physical access, including locked server rooms, cable management and secured equipment.
A network security device that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and decides whether to allow or block specific traffic based on a set of predefined security rules.
